item.title: Snowfall and clouds may slow East Antarctic ice loss in a warmer world
item.description: [Climate & Environment] Keyword: climate change — A new modeling study, published in the journal Nature Climate Change, suggests that the East Antarctic Ice Sheet may be more resilient to extreme long-term warming than previously estimated. Increased snowfall, greater cloud cover and changes in atmospheric circulation could partially offset ice loss—even under very high carbon dioxide concentrations.

item.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
item.description: [Climate & Environment] Keyword: global warming — Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

item.title: Marine fossils in Colombia reveal possible evolutionary transition without mass extinction
item.description: [Open Source Software] Keyword: FOSS — A remarkably diverse fossil ecosystem in central Colombia that preserves an unusual overlap between survivors of older Jurassic groups and newer Cretaceous lineages has led researchers at McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) to recognize a new pattern of large-scale evolutionary transition, one that does not include mass extinctions.

item.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
item.description: [Open Source Software] Keyword: FOSS — Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
item.description: [Diabetes & Kidney Disease] Keyword: type 2 diabetes — A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
